blocks.text: Blood capillaries deliver oxygen to the tissues and remove carbon dioxide from tissues. The partial pressure of CO₂ is higher in tissues than in blood. It causes the carbon dioxide to enter from tissues into blood. While, the process reverses in lungs where the partial pressure of CO₂ is lower in alveoli than in blood. Blood transports carbon dioxide from tissues to lugs in three ways.

Approximately 72% of carbon dioxide is carried in the blood as bicarbonate ions. CO₂ enters the RBCs and combines with water to form carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) in the presence of enzyme carbonic anhydrase. Carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) disassociates to form hydrogen ions (H⁺) and bicarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻). The hydrogen ion readily associates with oxyhaemoglobin and oxygen of oxyhaemoglobin is released to the tissue. While the bicarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻) moves out from RBCs into plasma. The movement of bicarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻) is facilitated by a transporter that exchanges one chloride ion (Cl⁻) for a bicarbonate ion (this is called the “chloride shift” or “Hamburger phenomenon”).
The formation of carbonic acid is important in maintaining the acid-base balance of the blood, because bicarbonate serves as the major buffer of the blood plasma.
About 20% of CO₂ is carried as carboxyhaemoglobin. When partial pressure of CO₂ is higher in blood than tissues, CO₂ combines with the globin chains of haemoglobin and forms carboxyhaemoglobin.

blocks.text: CO₂ binds to the protein portion of haemoglobin while O₂ binds to the haem irons. So, both do not compete for attachment to haemoglobin.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: CO₂ joined to the globin (protein) chains of haemoglobin is called carbaminohaemoglobin. Carboxyhaemoglobin is haemoglobin joined to carbon monoxide (CO), the cause of carbon monoxide poisoning. The book also reverses the direction: CO₂ joins haemoglobin in the tissues, where the partial pressure of CO₂ is higher in the tissues than in blood (as the first paragraph says), so CO₂ enters the blood and combines with the globin chains.
When CO₂ enters blood, a little amount dissolves in the water of blood plasma. About 8% of CO₂ is carried this way.

The blood carries CO₂ in these three forms to the lungs. The lower PCO₂ of the air inside the alveoli causes the conversion of H₂CO₃ into H₂O and CO₂. The CO₂ diffuses out of blood into the alveoli, so that it can leave the body in the next exhalation.

blocks.alt: Two panels side by side. Left, at the tissues: carbon dioxide from the tissue cells crosses the capillary wall; some dissolves in plasma, some combines with haemoglobin in a red blood cell, and some combines with water (carbonic anhydrase) to form carbonic acid, which gives hydrogen ions (they combine with Hb) and bicarbonate ions; bicarbonate leaves the RBC as chloride enters. Right, at the alveoli: the reactions run in reverse and carbon dioxide diffuses out into the alveoli.

Right, at the alveoli: the reactions run in reverse and carbon dioxide diffuses out into the alveoli; bicarbonate enters the RBC and chloride leaves.

blocks.title: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning
blocks.text: Incomplete combustion of fuels such as wood, gasoline, propane, or natural gas produces CO gas. If gas heaters are left burning overnight in closed environments, CO accumulates in the room. It enters the body through inhalation and binds to haemoglobin with a much higher affinity than oxygen. This binding reduces the amount of haemoglobin available to transport oxygen to the body's tissues, leading to tissue hypoxia (oxygen deprivation). It leads to CO poisoning. Symptoms of CO poisoning may include headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea, confusion, shortness of breath, chest pain, and loss of consciousness. In severe cases, it can cause permanent brain damage, and even death.
